claims.text: Wear resistance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed primarily by formation of an in-situ, self-adaptive nanocrystalline oxide glaze.
The oxide glaze reduces adhesive and abrasive wear by protecting the friction interface.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn is a multielement alloy whose surface oxidation behavior depends on the redox tendencies of its constituent elements.
Changing the concentration of Cr or another oxygen-reactive element will alter oxide-glaze formation during wear.
The proposed oxide-glaze mechanism governs sliding wear from room temperature to approximately 800 degrees Celsius.
Sliding produces a thin, adherent nanocrystalline oxide glaze.
Networked intermetallic phases may coexist with, and contribute alongside, the oxide-glaze mediator.
Redox-active alloying elements preferentially oxidize during sliding.
A dense nanocrystalline glaze minimizes direct metallic contact and adhesive wear.
The oxide glaze redistributes frictional stresses.
At higher stress or temperature, the oxide layer becomes denser or reconfigures to maintain protection.
Increasing the concentration of redox-active elements will produce a thicker and more robust oxide glaze.
An oxygen-rich wear environment will produce a thicker and more robust oxide glaze than ambient oxygen.
A thicker and more robust oxide glaze will lower both friction coefficient and wear volume.
Reducing redox-active-element content or using an inert atmosphere will weaken oxide-layer formation and increase wear.
The mechanism should transfer to high-entropy-alloy coatings having similar multielement solid solutions and redox-active-element levels under industrial wear conditions.
The mechanism may cease to apply when processing or atmosphere prevents oxide formation.
Solid-solution strengthening and precipitation hardening by phases such as Laves phases may also affect coating wear performance.
